transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-14 16:00 PDT
- Duration: 54 minutes
- Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Dr. Asha Rao, Ben Torres, Claire Zhou (Kynno)

Summary:
Quick scoping for a 6-week POC focused on quality evaluation (golden prompts, hallucination checks), regression tests, and load/benchmark sizing. Customer emphasized strict hallucination tolerances for clinical summaries and need for per-prompt scoring. Discussed mixing hosted + dedicated fallback for peak hours.

Topics: golden prompts, scoring rubric, regression playlist, hallucination detection heuristics, bench load profile, timeline/milestones, security prerequisites (SOC2/KMS/SAML)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Liam Chen: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro — im Liam from Redwood, with Sofia our solutions engineer, you can, uh, go around real quick?
[00:08] Dr. Asha Rao: sure hi i'm asha, head of ml at kynno, we own the clinical summarization pipeline — we're validating an LLM assist feature for discharge summaries.
[00:14] Ben Torres: ben, infra lead — i'll own the benchmarking and run the load tests inside our VPC.
[00:18] Claire Zhou: claire, product — i'm focused on acceptance criteria and timelines.
[00:22] Sofia Martinez: great glad to be here. quick note, we'll propose a golden-prompt approach and a regression playlist tied to your golden set, and then run token-level latency and hallucination checks.
[00:33] Liam Chen: question to start — what does success look like? Claire?
[00:36] Claire Zhou: success for us is three things: 1) hallucinations under 1% on clinical-critical fields, 2) P95 latency < 600ms for our 1.2k token median case, and 3) no functional regressions across weekly model rollouts. also, cost targets were mentioned but secondary.
[00:52] Dr. Asha Rao: yeah and to add, hallucinations are non-negotiable for diagnosis or meds lines — even a single hallucinated med is a failure. we want deterministic checks, not just human review.
[01:05] Ben Torres: on load — nominal is ~15 tps during day, peak 60 tps for 10 minutes bursts; avg payload 1.5k tokens, 95th around 4k tokens with attachments. we need to size kv cache and batching accordingly.
[01:21] Sofia Martinez: helpful. we'll capture a realistic seq length distribution — Sofia explains: we usually test three buckets: short (under 512), medium (512-2k), long (2k-6k). Our runtime supports continuous batching and prefix caching which should help cost while keeping P95 low.
[01:36] Speaker 2: (inaudible) caching — is that prefix KV cache?
[01:39] Sofia Martinez: yes prefix KV cache, plus optional reuse across sessions when context matches. there can be tradeoffs if customers use private deployments and strict privacy configs — caching policies are configurable.
[01:48] Liam Chen: let's talk golden prompts. we recommend 200 golden prompts spanning positive/neutral/edge cases, and 50 adversarial prompts we call the 'hallucination stress set'. for scoring we score each output on a 1-5 rubric: factuality, format, completeness, safety. then aggregate by weighted mean.
[02:04] Dr. Asha Rao: can we see an example rubric? we need to map rubric to pass/fail per-summary. eg any factuality < 4 is fail for clinical fields.
[02:12] Liam Chen: yep we'll send the template; in practice customers often require binary gating for some fields (meds/diagnosis) and fuzzy scoring for narrative sections.
[02:20] Claire Zhou: how do you detect hallucinations automatically?
[02:23] Sofia Martinez: two-layer approach: heuristics + model-based checks. heuristics include entity mismatch, unexpected numeric ranges, and citation checks. model-based is a verification model (reranker) that compares claim tokens to source EHR segments. note: the verification model itself must be validated.
[02:39] Ben Torres: are these checks run inline or as async post-process?
[02:42] Sofia Martinez: both options. inline adds latency; our suggested pattern: quick heuristics inline to block obvious fails, full verification async with rollback/alert. for high-stakes lines we recommend inline fail-stop.
[02:55] Liam Chen: timeline — proposed POC is 6 weeks: week 0-1 data onboarding and golden set creation, week 2 benchmark and load validation, weeks 3-4 golden set regression runs and hallucination tuning, week 5-6 stabilization and handoff + docs. is that workable?
[03:13] Claire Zhou: that seems fine but we need a mid-point check at week 3 with engineering to decide on dedicated capacity.
[03:19] Liam Chen: agreed. on dedicated vs hosted: we can run early phase on hosted to move fast then switch to dedicated pools if latency or data isolation requires it. dedicated gives predictable throughput and VPC options but requires some lead time for capacity reservation.
[03:32] Dr. Asha Rao: what's the typical lead time?
[03:34] Sofia Martinez: reserved capacity lead time depends on region and GPU availability — usually 2-3 weeks to spin up and validate. we can schedule canary capacity earlier if needed.
[03:42] Ben Torres: for the benchmark, what metrics will you collect?
[03:45] Sofia Martinez: token-level latency, P50/P95/P99, tokens-per-second, GPU utilization, cost per 1k tokens, cache hit ratio, and hallucination false positive/negative rates vs human labels. we'll provide a spreadsheet with expected columns.
[04:00] Liam Chen: measurement detail — for hallucination rate we need a consistent labeling guideline. propose: label at field-level (meds/diagnosis/plan), binary flag plus severity. then compute field-level error rate and document examples.
[04:12] Dr. Asha Rao: agreed. how many labels do you need?
[04:14] Sofia Martinez: for meaningful statistics, at least 300 labeled examples per critical field for initial runs; 1k is better to establish confidence intervals. for POC we can start with 300 and expand post-POC.
[04:27] Claire Zhou: costs — can you give a ballpark for running our nominal week of tests?
[04:30] Liam Chen: rough estimate depends on model choice and quantization. we'll send a short TCO estimate: hosted baseline vs dedicated amortized monthly including burst capacity.
[04:39] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[04:40] Ben Torres: security items — SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration for private deployments, audit logs retention. we need SOC2 + encryption-in-transit+at-rest.
[04:49] Liam Chen: Redwood supports SOC2, SAML SSO, and our Private product integrates with customer KMS/HSM. we'll attach security pack and a checklist.
[04:57] Dr. Asha Rao: any limitations with our EHR data containing PHI? we need assurances for handling PHI in hosted mode.
[05:03] Sofia Martinez: hosted can be configured with strict retention and opt-out but for PHI we often recommend Private deployment — either VPC or on-prem — to meet compliance. we'll map options in the security doc.
[05:13] Liam Chen: demo-style question — can we run an early smoke using 20 queries to validate end-to-end?
[05:17] Ben Torres: yes we can provision an env for that; i'll supply a small dataset.
[05:20] Claire Zhou: how does regression testing integrate with our CI?
[05:23] Sofia Martinez: we provide an API and a regression runner that can be invoked from CI; outputs include diffs, score deltas, and flagged hallucinations. many customers run nightly golden-set checks.
[05:33] Liam Chen: risk items — note that verification models can themselves drift; include periodic calibration in the plan. also note long-context edge cases may increase cost; we'll document tradeoffs.
[05:44] Dr. Asha Rao: final question on scoring: can we weight fields? meds=high, diagnosis=high, plan=n medium, narrative low?
[05:51] Liam Chen: yes weights are configurable in the rubric; we'll propose a default mapping you can adjust.
[05:57] Claire Zhou: ok that's helpful. next steps recap?
[06:00] Liam Chen: recap: we'll send golden-prompt template, scoring rubric, preliminary cost comparison, and security checklist. Kynno to send samples and confirm SLOs. schedule benchmark kick-off.
[06:10] Claire Zhou: sounds good. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
